Internal benchmarking of officers

Source: R/ibench.R
ibench.Rd

Asks whether an officer stops more people of a group (or searches, arrests, uses force more often) than other officers do in the same circumstances. Officers work different places and hours, so each officer's stops are compared not with all other stops but with the other officers' stops weighted to look like this officer's: the propensity e(x) that a stop with circumstances x (place, hour, day, reason) is this officer's comes from a logistic regression on x (over all stops), and each other officer's stop gets the weight e / (1 - e), the weights of the effect on the treated (Ridgeway and MacDonald 2009). The benchmark is the weighted share of the outcome among those stops, and the z statistic compares the officer's share with it, with the variance of a proportion for the officer and, for the benchmark, that of a proportion over its effective number of stops, (sum w)^2 / sum w^2. With many officers some will stand out by chance: q is the false discovery rate of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) over the officers tested, and flag marks those with q below fdr.

Usage

ibench(y, off, x = NULL, minn = 20, fdr = 0.05, dr = FALSE, local = FALSE)

Arguments

y

The outcome of each stop: 0 or 1 (or FALSE or TRUE), such as whether the person stopped belongs to the group of interest.

off

The officer of each stop: labels, two officers at least.

x

NULL or the circumstances of each stop: a numeric matrix, a data frame or list of numeric columns, or one numeric vector, one row per stop (code a place or an hour as indicator columns).

minn

The fewest stops of an officer to test: one whole number from 1.

fdr

The false discovery rate at which an officer is flagged: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

dr

TRUE for the doubly robust benchmark, FALSE for the propensity weights alone.

local

TRUE to estimate the local false discovery rate and flag by it.

Value

An object of class ibench, a list: tab, one row per officer (off, n stops, rate, the officer's share of the outcome, bench, the benchmark, ess, its effective number of stops, z, p, q, with local lfdr, and flag); fdr; minn; nx, the number of columns of x; dr; and null, NULL without local, otherwise the empirical null's delta, sigma and p0.

Details

Two options follow Ridgeway and MacDonald (2009) further:

  • dr = TRUE, the doubly robust benchmark: the propensity weights are kept, and a logistic regression of the outcome on an indicator of the officer's stops and on x, weighted 1 for the officer's stops and e / (1 - e) for the others, adjusts for what the weights leave unbalanced. The benchmark is the mean of its fitted chances for the officer's stops with the indicator set to 0 (the same stops made by the others), and z is the officer's rate less the benchmark over the sandwich (robust) standard error of that difference from the weighted fit. The estimate is right when either the propensity model or the outcome model is. This is the propensity-weighted regression of the first author's fastDR package (which fits the propensity by boosting, where a logistic regression is used here).

  • local = TRUE, the local false discovery rate of Efron (2004) for each tested officer: the chance that an officer with that z is one of the unremarkable majority. The density of all the officers' z is fitted by a Poisson regression on a natural spline of 7 df over a histogram of 120 breaks, the null density is a normal N(delta, sigma^2) fitted by maximum likelihood to the middle of the z values (the empirical null, which absorbs spread that the benchmark misses), and lfdr = p0 f0(z) / f(z), as in the defaults of the package locfdr; null gives delta, sigma and p0. flag then marks the officers with lfdr below fdr (Efron suggests 0.2). The method is meant for many officers, hundreds rather than tens; when the null cannot be fitted the function refuses.

The comparison is only as good as x: circumstances that differ between officers and are not in x are left in the difference. An officer with fewer than minn stops, or whose propensity model does not converge (circumstances that separate this officer's stops from all others), is not tested (NA).

References

Ridgeway, G. and MacDonald, J. M. (2009). Doubly robust internal benchmarking and false discovery rates for detecting racial bias in police stops. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 104(486), 661-668. doi:10.1198/jasa.2009.0034

Benjamini, Y. and Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57(1), 289-300. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x

Efron, B. (2004). Large-scale simultaneous hypothesis testing: the choice of a null hypothesis. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 99(465), 96-104. doi:10.1198/016214504000000089

Examples

set.seed(2)
n <- 3000
off <- sample(sprintf("o%02d", 1:12), n, TRUE)
night <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(off %in% c("o01", "o02"), 0.7, 0.3))
y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + night + 0.8 * (off == "o03")))
ibench(y, off, data.frame(night), minn = 50)
